summary: Lists DHCP option codes that were assigned to proposed options which were never used, and directs IANA to make them available for assignment to other options. It also lists several codes not currently documented in an RFC. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3679 sorts DHCP option codes into two groups: unused codes that can be assigned again and undocumented codes that should stay reserved. This helps keep the option registry accurate.

questions: which dhcp option codes are free
which dhcp option codes are unused
what dhcp option codes were reclaimed
why were dhcp option codes returned to iana
subtitle: DHCP option codes assigned to proposals that were never used and can be reassigned.

tldr.problem: Some DHCP option codes had been assigned to proposed options that were never used, while other undocumented codes were still in use.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists unused codes to return to IANA and separately identifies undocumented codes that should remain reserved.
tldr.outcome: IANA returned the listed values to the available pool under the procedures in RFC 2939. RFC 3679 has been updated by RFC 8910.

today: RFC 3679 is an Informational document and has been updated by RFC 8910.

sections.title: Why DHCP Option Codes Were Reviewed
sections.content:
Before the procedures in RFC 2489 and RFC 2939 were published, option codes had been assigned to proposed DHCP options that were never used. RFC 3679 lists those codes and directs IANA to make them available for future assignments.

The RFC also lists codes that were not documented in an RFC but should not be reassigned. Thus, absence of an RFC description alone does not mean a code is unused.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry had values reserved for options that never appeared. The memo identifies which values can be reused and which should stay reserved.

sections.title: Codes Returned for Reassignment
sections.content:
Section 2 lists codes and their proposed option names, prior documentation, contact information when known, and reason for recovery. The reasons include a proposal that expired, an option omitted from a published specification, or a proposal that was never published or used in general.

Examples include codes for a service-location naming authority, relay-agent options from an early draft, POSIX timezone, IPv6 transition, printer name, and DHCP failover. The memo records that the current failover protocol did not use a DHCP option.
sections.plainLanguage: Each returned code has a short explanation of what it had been intended for and why that assignment was no longer needed.

sections.title: Undocumented Codes That Remain Reserved
sections.content:
Some codes were still used despite lacking a published RFC. Codes used by the PXE specification and codes used by Apple devices remain on the IANA list while the DHC working group considers their disposition.

The document also discusses codes reserved for a possible option-code extension mechanism. It records other codes that had already been returned for reassignment before this RFC was published.
sections.plainLanguage: Some codes looked undocumented but were being used by existing systems. The memo keeps those codes reserved instead of treating them as free.

sections.title: IANA Action and Security Note
sections.content:
IANA returned the codes from Section 2 to the available DHCP option list. They may be assigned to new options under RFC 2939 procedures, after codes that were never assigned or were already returned have been exhausted.

The RFC says there are no known security implications because none of the reclaimed options are known to be in use.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA can assign the recovered codes to future options after other available values are used. The RFC reports no known security impact from this cleanup.

references.text: Patrick, M., "DHCP Relay Agent Information Option", RFC 3046, January 2001.
Droms, R., "Procedures and IANA Guidelines for Definition of New DHCP Options and Message Types", BCP 43, RFC 2939, September 2000.
